question: What is the primary purpose of disaster monitoring in nursing?

options.A: Writing historical books about past weather events
options.B: Systematically collecting and analyzing data during crises
options.C: Punishing facilities that fail to prepare for emergencies
options.D: Replacing the role of physicians in emergency rooms

explanation: Disaster monitoring is all about watching, gathering, and studying information so healthcare workers can respond effectively to emergencies. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h1)

question: How does a nurse's role change during disaster monitoring compared to routine bedside care?

options.A: The focus shifts toward population health and community-wide safety
options.B: Nurses stop caring for individual patients entirely
options.C: Administrative paperwork replaces all hands-on nursing duties
options.D: Clinical assessment skills are no longer needed in the field

explanation: While bedside care focuses on one patient at a time, disaster monitoring broadens the nurse's view to entire communities and resource tracking. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h1)

question: Which phase of disaster monitoring involves watching weather patterns and community vulnerabilities before an event hits?
explanation: The pre-disaster phase focuses on preparation, tracking risks, and looking at weather or health data before a crisis occurs. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h2)

question: What is a nurse primarily monitoring during the trans-disaster phase?

options.A: Historical trends of past earthquakes over fifty years
options.B: Routine annual budget reports for hospital supplies
options.C: Real-time casualties, bed availability, and active environmental hazards
options.D: Long-term economic recovery and rebuilding costs

explanation: The trans-disaster phase happens right during the event, requiring immediate tracking of injuries, hospital space, and ongoing dangers. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h2)

question: What is the main function of an early warning system in a disaster context?

options.A: Calculating the financial cost of destroyed property
options.B: Treating injuries after a building collapses
options.C: Detecting threats early before they cause widespread harm
options.D: Punishing individuals who ignore safety rules

explanation: Early warning systems use technology and data to spot danger ahead of time so people can prepare and evacuate. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h3)

question: A nurse notices a sudden cluster of patients arriving with severe vomiting and diarrhea from the same neighborhood. What action best reflects hazard identification?

options.A: Asking the hospital finance department to buy more IV fluids
options.B: Waiting until next week to see if more people show up at the clinic
options.C: Reporting the unusual disease pattern to public health authorities immediately
options.D: Telling the patients it is just a normal stomach flu and sending them home

explanation: Spotting unusual symptom clusters and alerting authorities helps catch outbreaks early before they turn into major disasters. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h3)

question: What does syndromic surveillance primarily track during a health emergency?

options.A: Only confirmed laboratory cases of rare tropical diseases
options.B: Hospital staff attendance records during a night shift
options.C: Groups of symptoms before laboratory tests are confirmed
options.D: The exact financial cost of medical equipment used

explanation: Syndromic surveillance watches symptom patterns early on, allowing teams to act fast without waiting for slow lab test results. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h4)

question: Why is using standardized definitions for injuries and symptoms crucial during a disaster?

options.A: It stops patients from complaining about long waiting times
options.B: It allows doctors to avoid writing detailed patient progress notes
options.C: It reduces the total number of patients admitted to the hospital
options.D: It ensures that data collected from different clinics can be accurately combined

explanation: When everyone uses the same definitions, health authorities can trust the combined numbers from multiple clinics and hospitals. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h4)

question: Which of the following is an example of resource tracking during a disaster?

options.A: Counting how many hours of sleep nurses got last night
options.B: Interviewing community leaders about past local floods
options.C: Predicting what the weather will look like next month
options.D: Monitoring available hospital beds and oxygen tank supplies

explanation: Resource tracking keeps an active count of vital physical items and space needed to care for incoming patients. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h5)

question: What is a major risk of failing to monitor resource logistics actively during a crisis?

options.A: Patients recovering much faster than expected
options.B: Lower hospital electricity bills for the month
options.C: Too many medical supplies cluttering the hallways
options.D: Unexpected stockouts that halt life-saving treatments

explanation: Without active tracking, hospitals run out of critical items like oxygen or IV fluids right when demand is highest. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h5)

question: What communication tool helps nurses pass structured and concise patient or situation data during a crisis?

options.A: Casual text messages sent without checking details
options.C: Complex medical research articles from foreign journals
options.D: Long narrative diary entries written at the end of the shift

explanation: SBAR gives healthcare workers a quick, organized way to share essential facts without wasting time during emergencies. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h6)

question: Why is it important to avoid heavy clinical jargon when reporting disaster monitoring data to non-medical coordinators?

options.A: To ensure disaster coordinators understand the message and act on it quickly
options.B: To make the report look less professional and more casual
options.C: Because clinical terms are illegal to use outside of hospital buildings
options.D: Because non-medical personnel are not allowed to hear health statistics

explanation: Clear, plain language prevents dangerous misunderstandings between health workers and municipal response teams. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h6)

question: What ethical balance must nurses maintain while collecting data during a disaster?

options.A: Balancing hospital profits with the cost of medical textbooks
options.B: Balancing nursing working hours with physician holiday schedules
options.C: Balancing public health surveillance needs with patient privacy and confidentiality
options.D: Balancing local laws with international travel restrictions

explanation: Nurses must track outbreaks to protect the public while still respecting each patient's right to private medical information. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h7)

question: Which of the following actions is NOT legally or ethically acceptable when monitoring a public health crisis?

options.A: Ensuring fair distribution of available medical supplies to all patients
options.B: Tracking the total number of cholera cases admitted to the ward
options.C: Reporting anonymous symptom data to the local ministry of health
options.D: Broadcasting identifiable personal details of patients on public social media

explanation: Sharing private patient names and identifying details publicly violates confidentiality laws and ethical nursing standards. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of a post-disaster debriefing or hot wash session?

options.A: Calculating annual bonuses for hospital administrators
options.B: Analyzing what went well and where emergency processes failed
options.C: Assigning blame to individual nurses who made mistakes
options.D: Destroying all medical records from the disaster period

explanation: Debriefings review the response objectively so the healthcare team can learn and improve for future emergencies. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h8)

question: How do post-disaster evaluation data directly benefit future community health responses?

options.A: By guiding updates to emergency action plans and preparedness training
options.B: By proving that disasters can be completely prevented from ever happening
options.C: By reducing the number of nurses required on future hospital shifts
options.D: By eliminating the need for any future weather monitoring equipment

explanation: Learning from past mistakes allows hospitals to update their disaster plans and train staff more effectively for next time. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h8)
